g1.correct: they rarely seem to count, even though adults call teenagers ‘the future’
accept: they rarely seem to count, even though adults call teenagers ‘the future’
g1.label: 1. According to the writer, what usually happens to teenagers’ opinions about the present?
g1.why: The second paragraph says adults call teenagers “the future” but our opinions about the present rarely seem to count.

g2.correct: a teacher, a psychologist, or a worried parent
accept: a teacher, a psychologist, or a worried parent
g2.label: 2. Who does the writer say usually gets interviewed instead of teenagers, on topics like climate change or mental health?
g2.why: The text names exactly these three as the people usually interviewed instead of the teenagers actually living through the issue.

g3.correct: no editor can cut or change their opinion before it reaches the reader
accept: no editor can cut or change their opinion before it reaches the reader
g3.label: 3. Why does the writer say blogs matter to them?
g3.why: The third paragraph says nobody edits the writer’s opinion or cuts their sentence short, so the reader gets it unfiltered.

g4.correct: to read a post by someone under eighteen properly instead of assuming it matters less
accept: to read a post by someone under eighteen properly instead of assuming it matters less
g4.label: 4. What challenge does the writer set for the reader at the end of the post?
g4.why: The final paragraph asks the reader not to assume a young writer’s post matters less, and to read it properly instead.

g5.correct: to draw the reader in personally with a rhetorical question — a typical way to open a blog post
accept: to draw the reader in personally with a rhetorical question — a typical way to open a blog post
g5.label: 5. Why does the writer open with a rhetorical question instead of a plain statement?
g5.why: Opening with a question that speaks directly to the reader’s own experience is a common blog technique for creating a personal hook.

g6.correct: a personal, conversational tone that is typical of blog register, rather than a distant, formal one
accept: a personal, conversational tone that is typical of blog register, rather than a distant, formal one
g6.label: 6. What effect does addressing the reader directly with “you” create?
g6.why: Direct address (“you”, “you’d”, “you’re”) is a blog-register feature that makes writing feel personal and conversational, unlike the distant tone of a formal essay.

g1.correct: I think it's time the school took a closer look at this policy.
accept: I think it's time the school took a closer look at this policy.
g1.label: 1. Introducing an opinion about a new school policy — which version sounds like a blog post?
g1.why: It's clear, personal (“I think”) and direct — blog register is informal but still well-organised, unlike the stiff, impersonal formal option or the slangy casual one.

g2.correct: In my opinion, phones could actually help us learn — if we use them the right way.
accept: In my opinion, phones could actually help us learn — if we use them the right way.
g2.label: 2. Introducing an opinion about phones in class — which version sounds like a blog post?
g2.why: It states a personal opinion plainly and clearly, without the passive, over-formal phrasing of the essay-style option or the dismissive slang of the casual one.

accept: Here's something worth thinking about.
g3.label: 3. Inviting the reader to think about an idea — which version sounds like a blog post?
g3.why: It's short, direct and speaks to the reader informally, rather than using the stiff “the reader is hereby invited” phrasing or slang like “fr fr”.

g4.correct: I've noticed how much peer pressure affects the choices we make.
accept: I've noticed how much peer pressure affects the choices we make.
g4.label: 4. Giving a personal example about peer pressure — which version sounds like a blog post?
g4.why: It uses “I've noticed” — personal and clear — rather than the academic “it has been observed by this author” or the vague slang version.

g5.correct: What do you think? Let me know in the comments.
accept: What do you think? Let me know in the comments.
g5.label: 5. Ending with a call to action — which version sounds like a blog post?
g5.why: It directly invites the reader to respond, which is exactly what a call-to-action closing does — the formal option is stiff and the casual one sounds dismissive.

g6.correct: Most teenagers use social media every day — and I'm one of them.
accept: Most teenagers use social media every day — and I'm one of them.
g6.label: 6. Making a claim with evidence — which version sounds like a blog post?
g6.why: It makes the claim clearly and adds a personal note, unlike the over-formal “according to statistical data” or the vague, slangy option.

g7.correct: I have to disagree with that idea, and here's why.
accept: I have to disagree with that idea, and here's why.
g7.label: 7. Expressing disagreement — which version sounds like a blog post?
g7.why: It disagrees clearly and promises a reason, matching blog register — the formal option is overly stiff and the casual one gives no reason at all.

g8.correct: Ignored by adults, many teenagers turn to blogging instead.
accept: Ignored by adults, many teenagers turn to blogging instead.
g8.label: 8. Review — which sentence correctly begins with a participle construction?
g8.why: This reviews participle constructions from 10g-participle-writing: the opening participle must be the past participle “Ignored” (teenagers ARE ignored), not the base form “Ignore” or the wrong -ing form “Ignoring”, which would mean teenagers do the ignoring.

accept: Opening hook
g1.label: 1. “Ever wondered why nobody at school ever asks what students actually want?”
g1.why: A question that grabs the reader’s attention right at the start is a classic opening hook, not yet stating an opinion or giving evidence.

accept: Thesis (main opinion)
g2.label: 2. “I believe students should have a real vote in decisions that affect their own school day.”
g2.why: This states the writer's central opinion directly (“I believe…should”), which is exactly what a thesis statement does.

accept: Opening hook
g3.label: 3. “Have you ever felt like your opinion didn’t matter, just because of your age?”
g3.why: Like item 1, this is a question designed to pull the reader in personally before any opinion or evidence is given — an opening hook.

accept: Supporting point
g4.label: 4. “For example, my school changed the lunch menu last term without asking a single student what they thought.”
g4.why: “For example” signals a concrete piece of evidence backing up the writer's opinion — that is a supporting point, not the opinion itself.

accept: Call-to-action closing
g5.label: 5. “So next time there’s a school survey, don’t skip it — your answer could actually change something.”
g5.why: This tells the reader what to do next, which is the job of a call-to-action closing at the end of a blog post.

accept: Thesis (main opinion)
g6.label: 6. “In my view, teenagers understand school life better than most adults realise.”
g6.why: “In my view” signals the writer's central opinion, making this a thesis statement rather than a hook or a piece of evidence.

accept: Supporting point
g7.label: 7. “A recent survey at my school found that 80% of students wanted more say in homework deadlines — but nobody followed up on it.”
g7.why: This gives concrete evidence (a survey statistic) to back up the writer's opinion, which is exactly what a supporting point does.

accept: Call-to-action closing
g8.label: 8. “Comment below and tell me: should students get a vote on this too?”
g8.why: This directly asks the reader to respond, which marks it as a call-to-action closing rather than a hook, thesis or supporting point.
